newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Big Belgian bank merger seen only matter of time.
newsitem.headline: Big Belgian bank merger seen only matter of time.

text.p: The Belgian banking sector is moving inexorably towards concentration in the run-up to European economic and monetary union (EMU), analysts and top industry executives said on Thursday.

"(In Belgium) there are too many banks and none which can compete on a European level. If we can merge two to get a big bank at a European level it makes a lot of sense," Jean-Pierre Gerard, Chief Executive Officer of Belgian insurance company Royale Belge, told a news conference on its results.

Merger speculation has long centred on Belgium's biggest bank Generale Bank and number four Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL). At earnings news conferences this week, the banks' chiefs did not completely rule out the idea of a "Big Belgian Bank".
The number two Dexia CC already has a cross border link with Credit Local de France and the number three Kredietbank reiterated on Thursday it was happy on its own.
It also denied market talk that it was in merger talks with French Credit Commercial de France, adding that both banks had been "good friends" for many years.

Asked about the possibility that Generale Bank and BBL could merge, Kredietbank Chief Executive Officer Marcel Cockaerts said: "We would have no problem with a 'Big Belgian Bank'. We will be happy to be the 'Fast Other Bank'."

Analysts said what is driving the urge to get together is the need for economies of scale, particularly on the run up to the introduction of a single European currency in 1999, the cost of which is forecast to be huge.

In January Etienne Davignon, chairman of Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB), Generale bank's parent, said a merger with BBL was still an attractive business proposition despite the fact a similar move was blocked last year by BBL shareholder ING.

A Brussels-based foreign banker later drew attention to the need for concentration by saying Belgium needed European-sized banks with assets of at least $500 billion. All four top Belgian banks would have to link up to create a bank of that size.
Gerard said Royale Belge, which owns around 12.4 percent of BBL, also supported the idea of a large merger in the Belgian banking sector, but did not know if it would come about.

The renewed merger talk has sparked a wave of buying of top bank shares. Generale Bank shares dropped 175 francs to 13,525 on Thursday, but dealers said the mark-down represented a bout of profit-taking rather than a reversal of views on the sector. BBL ended down 20 francs at 8,340 francs.

"The banks which have the most to benefit from the speculation are coming back a bit. It's not because of denials or because the market is disappointed that nothing has been announced yet," said an analyst at brokerage Petercam.
There were very few sellers of bank shares. "Investors who are convinced of the (merger) story wouldn't sell now," he said.
Dealers said bank shares were not overvalued. Generale Bank and BBL, which have seen rises of almost 14 percent since the end of February, were not likely to suffer dramatic falls.
Some analysts said however a merger could be costly and it would be difficult to blend two long-standing rivals such as Generale Bank and BBL.
Dealers said that if a merger was on the cards it would not be announced soon because of unrest in Belgium over job losses and the inevitability that such a merger would force layoffs.
"It would take a very long time to integrate two different institutions and only show profitability in the medium to long term," said the Petercam analyst.
Belgian media have speculated that Belgian financier Albert Frere is a driving force behind a Generale/BBL merger.
Frere, who controls Groupe Bruxelles Lambert (GBL), BBL's parent company, recently bought into the capital of Cie de Suez, the French group which controls Societe Generale de Belgique.
A merger between BBL and Generale would enable Frere to cash in on his BBL shares.
